h1: Moving from FMCG sales to beer sales
title: Moving from FMCG Sales to Beer Sales | Craft Beer School
desc: What carries over from FMCG sales into beer sales in India, what changes with excise and outlet licensing and how to prepare for the interview.
teaser: FMCG sellers know distribution. Beer adds excise, licensed outlets and a product that goes stale.
standfirst: FMCG sales experience is one of the most common routes into beer sales. Much of it transfers directly. The parts that do not transfer are regulation, the outlet and the product itself. Interviewers probe those.
sections: Your distribution skills carry straight across

Beat planning, distributor management, secondary sales, stock norms, schemes, visibility and collections: if you have done these for biscuits, soap or soft drinks, you already speak most of the language of beer sales. Many beer companies actively recruit from FMCG for exactly that reason.

The trade runs on the same principles. Get the product into the right outlets, keep it in stock, make it visible and get paid. A sales officer who can manage a distributor's credit and run an outlet audit is valuable in any category.
Regulation changes the shape of the job

The biggest difference is that alcohol in India is controlled mostly by states. Excise duty, pricing, licensing of outlets, permitted pack sizes and even who may act as wholesaler differ from state to state. In some states a government corporation handles wholesale. In others private distributors do. Rules change through notifications, so the sales team works closely with the company's regulatory people.

In practice this means you cannot simply open new outlets as you would with a general store. Every bar, restaurant and shop needs the right licence. Schemes and promotions are also limited by state rules. Learn the rules in the state you would cover before the interview and say that you would confirm the current position with the regulatory team.

Direct alcohol advertising is restricted in India. That pushes much of the brand building onto the point of sale: the menu listing, the tap handle, the fridge, the staff recommendation. In beer, a sales person is also the brand's main voice in the outlet.

FMCG sellers used to TV support can find this a big change. The good news is that relationships with outlet owners and staff count for even more. You already have those skills.

Biscuits last months. Beer starts losing freshness from the day it is packaged. Heat speeds that up, which matters in Indian summers when trucks and shop storerooms can run well above 30 °C. Hop aroma fades. Stale, cardboard-like flavours appear. Unpasteurised craft beer in kegs is more delicate again and wants cold storage throughout.

That changes stock management. First expired, first out matters more than in most FMCG categories. A distributor who stacks beer in a hot godown is damaging your brand, not just holding stock. Our guide on brewery sales careers covers the craft side of this.

If the company sells draught beer, you will deal with kegs, dispense systems and line cleaning. A dirty line spoils good beer. Draught quality guidance commonly recommends cleaning lines at least every two weeks. You do not have to clean them yourself, but you must know when an outlet is not doing it and how to raise it without losing the account.

Kegs are also assets that cost money and must come back. Tracking keg returns is one of the less glamorous tasks in beer sales and one of the most important for the company's cash.

Expect the panel to test product knowledge as well as sales craft. Be ready to explain in simple words how beer is made, the difference between lager and ale and why freshness matters. Know the main styles on the market in your target city, from mainstream strong lagers to the wheat beers and IPAs on craft menus.

Bring numbers from your FMCG career that translate: outlets added, numeric distribution, sales growth, collections. Then show how you would apply the same approach inside the rules that govern alcohol. If you are weighing this move against others, moving from hospitality to brewery sales describes the route in from the other side of the bar.
Responsible selling is part of the job

You will be selling an age-restricted product. Never push volume in ways that encourage heavy drinking. Respect outlet rules on age checks. Many companies have their own responsible marketing codes and expect sales teams to follow them.

Your first step: visit five licensed outlets in your city this week. Note which beers are on the menu, how they are stored and what the staff say when asked for a recommendation. You will learn more about the job from that than from any job description.
faqs: Is FMCG experience useful for beer sales?
Very. Distribution, beat planning, distributor management and outlet relationships transfer directly. Regulation, freshness and draught are the main things to learn.
How is beer sales different from FMCG sales in India?
Alcohol is regulated state by state, outlets need licences, direct advertising is restricted and beer is a fresh product that suffers in heat.
Do beer sales reps need to know brewing?
A basic understanding helps a lot. Outlet staff and owners ask questions and a confident, accurate answer builds trust in the brand.
How often should draught lines be cleaned?
Draught quality guidance commonly recommends at least every two weeks. Dirty lines cause off-flavours that customers blame on the beer.
